claim: A total of 129 task-related neurons were recorded from the head of the caudate nucleus (1–5 mm anterior to the anterior commissure) in three monkeys.
source: A total of 129 task-related neurons were recorded from the head of the caudate nucleus (1–5 mm anterior to the anterior commissure, Figure 1C) in three monkeys.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data collection with specific anatomical location and sample size.

claim: 109 neurons showed firing modulation for each repetitive visual stimulus.
source: Of these, 109 neurons (52, 33 and 24 neurons from monkeys G, H and L, respectively) showed firing modulation for each repetitive visual stimulus, while the remaining neurons only exhibited a phasic activity associated with saccades (n = 15) or reward delivery (n = 3), or showed sustained activity in the middle of the stimulus sequence (n = 2).
evidence: Direct report of experimental observation with specific neuron counts.

claim: The majority of caudate neurons responding to repetitive stimuli (74%, 83/109) exhibited a gradual rise in firing modulation for each stimulus during the trial.
source: Like this example, the majority of caudate neurons responding to the repetitive stimuli (74%, 83/109) exhibited a gradual rise in firing modulation for each stimulus during the trial, while only one neuron responded roughly equally to each stimulus in the sequence.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of neuronal response patterns with specific percentages and counts.

claim: The neuronal activity of increase-type neurons peaked at 160 ± 75 ms (SD, n = 84) from the stimulus onset in trials with a 400 ms ISI.
source: On average, the neuronal activity of these increase-type neurons peaked at 160 ± 75 ms (SD, n = 84) from the stimulus onset in trials with a 400 ms ISI.
evidence: Statistical summary of timing measurements from experimental data.

claim: 88% (74/84) of increase-type neurons exhibited a transient activity around the time of saccades following the omission of regular stimulus.
source: Most of them (88%, 74/84) also exhibited a transient activity around the time of saccades following the omission of regular stimulus (Figure 2A, right panel, red trace).
evidence: Quantitative report of neuronal activity patterns with specific percentages.

claim: A minority of neurons (23%, 25/109) responded vigorously to the initial few stimuli in the sequence and exhibited a gradual decrease of activity.
source: As with another example shown in Figure 2B, a minority of neurons (23%, 25/109) responded vigorously to the initial few stimuli in the sequence and exhibited a gradual decrease of activity that eventually disappeared at the time of oddball (i.e. stimulus omission or deviation).
evidence: Quantitative description of a distinct neuronal response pattern.

claim: For decrease-type neurons, the response to the repetitive stimulus was greatest for the first stimulus, exhibiting a peak at 566 ± 358 ms (SD, n = 25) from the stimulus onset.
source: For all these decrease-type neurons, the response to the repetitive stimulus was greatest for the first stimulus, exhibiting a peak at 566 ± 358 ms (SD, n = 25) from the stimulus onset.
evidence: Statistical summary of timing measurements for a specific neuron type.

claim: The magnitude of neuronal activity for repetitive stimuli depended on the location of the saccade target in only 17% (14/84) of individual neurons.
source: The magnitude of neuronal activity for the repetitive stimuli depended on the location of the saccade target only in a minority of individual neurons (17%, 14/84, Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.05, 12 and 2 showed a preference for contralateral and ipsilateral targets, respectively, Figure 3C, filled circles), while there was a significant contralateral bias in the population (paired t-test, t83 = 3.40, p=0.005).
evidence: Statistical analysis of directional selectivity with specific test results.

claim: Neuronal activity in the missing oddball condition with the contralateral saccade target was approximately 5% greater than that with the ipsilateral saccade target.
source: When the magnitude of directional bias was quantified by computing a regression slope in Figure 3C, neuronal activity in the missing oddball condition with the contralateral saccade target was approximately 5% greater than that with the ipsilateral saccade target (slope = 1.08).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of directional bias using regression analysis.

claim: Neurons in the caudate nucleus exhibited greater firing modulation during the missing than the deviant oddball conditions.
source: As seen in Figure 2, neurons in the caudate nucleus exhibited greater firing modulation during the missing than the deviant oddball conditions.
evidence: Comparison of neuronal activity between experimental conditions with reference to figure.

claim: 50 out of 84 neurons showed differential activity between the missing and deviant conditions.
source: When the magnitude of neuronal activity was assessed by measuring the peak (100 ms bin) during 400 ms before the oddball (Figure 3A, black bar), 50 out of 84 neurons showed differential activity between the conditions (Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.05, Figure 3B, filled circles).
evidence: Statistical analysis of condition-dependent neuronal activity.

claim: In the population as a whole, the activity in the missing condition was approximately 1.7-fold greater than that in the deviant condition.
source: In the population as a whole, the activity in the missing condition was approximately 1.7-fold greater than that in the deviant condition (paired t-test, t83 = 11.7, p<10−19).
evidence: Statistical comparison of population activity between conditions.

claim: The peak activity gradually increased during stimulus repetition while the minimal value during each ISI remained almost unchanged throughout the trial in both oddball conditions.
source: Figure 3D plots the time courses of firing modulation for each repetitive stimulus, showing that the peak activity (data connected with solid lines) gradually increased during stimulus repetition while the minimal value during each ISI (100 ms bin, open symbols connected with dashed lines) remained almost unchanged throughout the trial in both oddball conditions.
evidence: Description of temporal dynamics of neuronal activity with reference to figure.

claim: Neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus showed periodic neuronal modulation that depended on the stimulus interval, showing a greater firing modulation for longer ISIs.
source: We previously demonstrated that the periodic neuronal modulation in the cerebellar dentate nucleus depended on the stimulus interval, showing a greater firing modulation for longer ISIs (Ohmae et al., 2013; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to previous published findings.

claim: The magnitude of periodic activity in the caudate nucleus altered as the ISI was systematically varied from 100 to 600 ms.
source: In this study, we also found that the magnitude of periodic activity in the caudate nucleus altered as the ISI was systematically varied from 100 to 600 ms.
evidence: Direct report of experimental observation.

claim: Among 49 increase-type neurons tested formally, the majority (76%, 37/49) were classified into long-tuned neurons.
source: Among 49 increase-type neurons tested formally, the majority (76%, 37/49) were classified into long-tuned neurons.
evidence: Quantitative classification of neuronal response properties.

claim: For long-tuned neurons, the normalized activities for the 100, 200, 300 and 400 ms ISIs were 9, 18, 43% and 64% of the response to the 600 ms ISI, respectively.
source: On average, the normalized activities for the 100, 200, 300 and 400 ms ISIs were 9, 18, 43% and 64% of the response to the 600 ms ISI, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative summary of duration tuning properties.

claim: A subset of caudate neurons (24%, 12/49) exhibited a preference for the medium ISIs.
source: We also found a subset of caudate neurons (24%, 12/49) exhibiting a preference for the medium ISIs like the one shown in Figure 4B.
evidence: Quantitative description of a distinct neuronal population.

claim: Almost all short-tuned neurons (92%, 11/12) exhibited maximal firing modulation for either 300 or 400 ms ISIs, and none showed a preference for the 100 ms ISI.
source: Almost all neurons (92%, 11/12) exhibited maximal firing modulation for either 300 or 400 ms ISIs, and none showed a preference for the 100 ms ISI.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of duration preference in a neuronal subpopulation.

claim: For short-tuned neurons, the magnitude of firing modulation was 15, 46, 88, 94% and 59% of the maximal value for the ISIs of 100, 200, 300, 400 and 600 ms, respectively.
source: In the population, the magnitude of firing modulation was 15, 46, 88, 94% and 59% of the maximal value for the ISIs of 100, 200, 300, 400 and 600 ms, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative summary of population tuning properties.

claim: Neurons in the caudate nucleus and the deep cerebellar nucleus exhibited periodic firing modulation for the isochronous visual stimuli, but the time courses of neuronal activity were quite different.
source: Although neurons in both the caudate nucleus and the deep cerebellar nucleus exhibited periodic firing modulation for the isochronous visual stimuli, the time courses of neuronal activity were quite different.
evidence: Comparative statement based on experimental observations.

claim: The neuronal firing in the caudate nucleus peaked approximately 160 ms after the stimulus onset and terminated at ~ 300 ms in trials with longer ISIs (300–600 ms).
source: The neuronal firing in the caudate nucleus peaked approximately 160 ms after the stimulus onset and terminated at ~ 300 ms in trials with longer ISIs (300–600 ms).
evidence: Quantitative description of temporal dynamics from experimental data.

claim: Neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited a transient decrement of activity that was lowest approximately 200 ms following the stimulus onset, and gradually resumed the firing rate until the time of the next stimulus.
source: In contrast, neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus reported previously (Ohmae et al., 2013; Figure 5C) exhibited a transient decrement of activity that was lowest approximately 200 ms following the stimulus onset, and gradually resumed the firing rate until the time of the next stimulus.
evidence: Description of temporal dynamics from previously published data.

claim: Neurons in the caudate nucleus and the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited firing modulation for the repetitive visual stimuli in opposite directions.
source: Thus, neurons in the caudate nucleus and the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited firing modulation for the repetitive visual stimuli in opposite directions, and the time courses of recovery from the transient activity for each stimulus clearly differed between the recording sites.
evidence: Comparative summary of experimental observations.

claim: The stimulus timing was better predicted by neuronal activity in the cerebellum than the caudate nucleus (mean Δt = 63 versus 28 ms).
source: Figure 5D plots the prediction errors in different interval conditions, showing that the stimulus timing was better predicted by neuronal activity in the cerebellum than the caudate nucleus (mean Δt = 63 versus 28 ms; bootstrap 95% CI [46, 81] and [14 44], respectively).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of temporal prediction accuracy with statistical confidence intervals.

claim: The cerebellum may carry more accurate temporal information than the striatum when predicting timing of periodic events.
source: These results suggest that the cerebellum may carry more accurate temporal information than the striatum when predicting timing of periodic events.
evidence: Interpretation based on the temporal prediction analysis results.

claim: Neuronal activity in the cerebellar nucleus at the time of stimulus omission correlated with saccade latency.
source: The previous study using the oddball detection task demonstrated that neuronal activity in the cerebellar nucleus at the time of stimulus omission correlated with saccade latency (Ohmae et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to previously published finding.

claim: The stochastic variation of saccade latency differently affected neuronal activity in the caudate and the cerebellar dentate nucleus.
source: The other study in our laboratory using the self-timing task showed that the stochastic variation of saccade latency differently affected neuronal activity in the caudate and the cerebellar dentate nucleus (Kunimatsu et al., 2018).
evidence: Reference to previously published finding.

claim: In the caudate nucleus, the population activities for different latency groups varied until just before saccade onsets (–161 ms).
source: In the caudate nucleus, the population activities for different latency groups varied until just before saccade onsets (–161 ms, Figure 6A, vertical dashed line), while neuronal activity around the time of saccades (±50 ms) were comparable between the groups (one-way ANOVA, p=0.90).
evidence: Statistical analysis of trial-by-trial variation in neuronal activity.

claim: The stochastic neuronal variation in the cerebellar nucleus disappeared well before saccade initiation (–428 ms).
source: In contrast, the stochastic neuronal variation in the cerebellar nucleus disappeared well before saccade initiation (–428 ms, Figure 6C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement of timing of neuronal variation.

claim: When the data were aligned with saccade initiation, the trial-by-trial variation disappeared earlier in the cerebellum than the caudate nucleus.
source: We evaluated the difference in timing of neuronal variation using the bootstrap procedure and found that when the data were aligned with saccade initiation the trial-by-trial variation disappeared earlier in the cerebellum than the caudate nucleus (Figure 6D).
evidence: Statistical comparison using bootstrap analysis.

claim: When the data were aligned with stimulus omission, the stochastic variation tended to emerge earlier in the cerebellum than the caudate nucleus.
source: When the same sets of data were aligned with the stimulus omission, the stochastic variation tended to emerge earlier in the cerebellum than the caudate nucleus (Figure 6B).
evidence: Comparative analysis of timing of neuronal variation.

claim: Neurons in the cerebellar nucleus exhibited trial-by-trial variation around the time of stimulus omission, while those in the caudate nucleus showed stochastic variation just before saccade initiation.
source: Thus, neurons in the cerebellar nucleus exhibited trial-by-trial variation around the time of stimulus omission, while those in the caudate nucleus showed stochastic variation just before saccade initiation.
evidence: Summary of comparative analysis of neuronal variation timing.

claim: The cerebellum might be responsible for the detection of stimulus omission, while the caudate nucleus might contribute to periodic saccade preparation.
source: Given that the reaction time in our behavioral paradigm depends both on the latencies of omission detection and saccade generation, the different timing of stochastic variation may indicate distinct roles of these subcortical structures; the cerebellum might be responsible for the detection of stimulus omission, while the caudate nucleus might contribute to periodic saccade preparation.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results suggesting functional roles.

claim: Electrical stimulation delivered 200 ms before the oddball promoted the detection of stimulus omission.
source: Although electrical stimulation delivered 200 ms before the oddball did not evoke immediate saccades, the detection of stimulus omission was clearly promoted (Figure 7A, red traces).
evidence: Direct observation from electrical stimulation experiment.

claim: The same stimulation pulses did not alter the detection of stimulus deviation in most of the stimulation experiments.
source: The same stimulation pulses did not alter the detection of stimulus deviation (blue traces) in this and most of the other stimulation experiments (see below).
evidence: Observation from electrical stimulation experiments.

claim: In 14 out of 29 sessions (48%), electrical stimulation significantly altered saccade latency for stimulus omission.
source: In 14 out of 29 sessions (48%), electrical stimulation significantly altered saccade latency (Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction), and the means of median latencies were significantly different in the population (paired t-test, t28 = 10.2, p<10−11).
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrical stimulation effects.

claim: Electrical stimulation reduced the variation of saccade latency for the stimulus omission in the population.
source: Furthermore, electrical stimulation also reduced the variation of saccade latency for the stimulus omission in the population (SDs averaged 58.0 ± 16.4 ms and 47.1 ± 13.1 ms, paired t-test, t57 = 3.45, p<0.005), while this effect was not observed in individual experiments (F-test, p>0.05, corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis of variability in behavioral responses.

claim: In trials with stimulus deviation, electrical stimulation failed to alter saccade latency in most of individual experiments (2/29, 7%) as well as in the population.
source: In contrast, in trials with stimulus deviation, electrical stimulation failed to alter saccade latency in most of individual experiments (2/29, 7%, Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.05, corrected) as well as in the population (paired t-test, t28 = 1.50, p=0.14, Figure 7D).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing lack of effect in specific condition.

claim: Electrical stimulation facilitated ipsiversive saccades in the missing condition.
source: Electrical stimulation facilitated ipsiversive saccades in the missing condition (5 out of 29 sessions, Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.05, corrected; in the population, paired t-test, t28 = 7.76, p<10−8), and also in the deviant condition to a lesser extent (1 out of 29, Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.05, corrected; in the population, paired t-test, t28 = 6.50, p<10−7).
evidence: Statistical analysis of directional effects of electrical stimulation.

claim: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant main effects of oddball condition and saccade direction, and interaction.
source: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant main effects (oddball condition, F1,84 = 118.28, p<0.05; saccade direction, F1,84 = 5.59, p<0.05) and interaction (F1,84 = 10.96, p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of factors affecting stimulation effects.

claim: Post hoc paired t-tests detected a significant difference between saccade directions in the missing but not in the deviant conditions.
source: Post hoc paired t-tests detected a significant difference between saccade directions in the missing but not in the deviant conditions (t28 = 3.23 and −1.51, p=0.005 and 0.14, respectively).
evidence: Statistical post-hoc analysis results.

claim: The neuronal signals in the caudate nucleus were involved in making decision in response to a single omission of a regular beat.
source: These results indicate that the neuronal signals in the caudate nucleus were involved in making decision in response to a single omission of a regular beat.
evidence: Interpretation of electrical stimulation results.

claim: Temporal information processing for periodic events differs from that for a single interval.
source: It has been suggested that temporal information processing for periodic events differs from that for a single interval, such as pressing a stopwatch at a specific time (Grahn and Brett, 2007; Grube et al., 2010; Patel and Iversen, 2014; Ross et al., 2018; Teki et al., 2011a; Teki et al., 2011b).
evidence: Reference to multiple published studies suggesting this distinction.

claim: Previous studies of functional imaging and clinical cases have elucidated brain regions relevant to rhythm processing in the frontoparietal cortices as well as in the basal ganglia and the cerebellum.
source: Previous studies of functional imaging (Aso et al., 2010; Grahn and Brett, 2007; Hove et al., 2013; Konoike et al., 2012; Teki and Griffiths, 2016) and clinical cases (Allman and Meck, 2012; Cope et al., 2014; Schlerf et al., 2007) have elucidated brain regions relevant to rhythm processing in the frontoparietal cortices as well as in the basal ganglia and the cerebellum.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The number of physiological studies in experimental animals examining rhythm processing are limited.
source: However, as the number of physiological studies in experimental animals are limited (Cadena-Valencia et al., 2018; Lakatos et al., 2008; Renoult et al., 2006), how individual neurons in these regions represent periodic timing remains largely unknown.
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature with citations.

claim: Most previous studies used timing tasks that required rhythmic movements, making it difficult to dissociate sensory from motor components in neuronal activity.
source: Furthermore, most of the previous studies used timing tasks that required rhythmic movements, making it difficult to dissociate sensory from motor components in neuronal activity (Bartolo et al., 2014; Merchant et al., 2011; Schneider and Ghose, 2012).
evidence: Critical assessment of previous research methodology with citations.

claim: The oddball detection paradigm requires temporal prediction of periodic events.
source: With the aim of clarifying the neuronal mechanism of rhythm processing, we have developed the oddball detection paradigm that requires temporal prediction of periodic events (Ohmae et al., 2013).
evidence: Description of the experimental paradigm with citation.

claim: To detect the stimulus omission, the subjects need to predict the timing of each stimulus in the sequence but are not allowed to make any movements until the omission.
source: Importantly, to detect the stimulus omission, the subjects need to predict the timing of each stimulus in the sequence but are not allowed to make any movements until the omission.
evidence: Description of task requirements.

claim: When tested in humans, the subjects relied on temporal prediction to detect the stimulus omission for sequences slower than 4 Hz, whereas they detected a slight stumbling of stimulus stream for faster sequences.
source: When tested in humans, the subjects indeed relied on temporal prediction to detect the stimulus omission for sequences slower than 4 Hz, whereas they detected a slight stumbling of stimulus stream for faster sequences (Ohmae and Tanaka, 2016).
evidence: Reference to previously published human behavioral study.

claim: Local inactivation and electrical stimulation applied to the cerebellar recording sites delayed and promoted the detection of the stimulus omission, respectively.
source: Because local inactivation and electrical stimulation applied to the recording sites delayed and promoted the detection of the stimulus omission, respectively, the periodic neuronal signals in the cerebellar nucleus likely contributed to the prediction of stimulus timing during the task (Ohmae and Tanaka, 2016; Ohmae et al., 2013; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: Reference to previously published causal manipulation experiments.

claim: The basal ganglia are essential for temporal information processing for both periodic and single event timing.
source: As above, evidence shows that the basal ganglia are also essential for temporal information processing for both periodic and single event timing (Buhusi and Meck, 2006; Coull et al., 2011; Merchant et al., 2013; Paton and Buonomano, 2018).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Dopamine signaling in the striatum appears to play a crucial role in regulating the signal flow in the cortico-basal ganglia pathways during timing tasks.
source: In particular, dopamine signaling in the striatum appears to play a crucial role in regulating the signal flow in the cortico-basal ganglia pathways during timing tasks (De Corte et al., 2019; Emmons et al., 2016; Kim and Narayanan, 2019; Kunimatsu and Tanaka, 2016; Soares et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies on dopamine's role.

claim: Neurons in the caudate nucleus exhibit periodic activity for isochronous repetitive visual stimuli, whereas the time courses of neuronal activity were clearly different from those in the cerebellum.
source: We show that neurons in the caudate nucleus also exhibit periodic activity for isochronous repetitive visual stimuli, whereas the time courses of neuronal activity were clearly different from those in the cerebellum.
evidence: Summary of main experimental findings.

claim: The caudate nucleus might be responsible for periodic motor preparation, while the cerebellar dentate nucleus may be involved in temporal prediction of periodic sensory event which is necessary to detect the stimulus omission.
source: Further quantitative analyses suggest that the caudate nucleus might be responsible for periodic motor preparation, while the cerebellar dentate nucleus may be involved in temporal prediction of periodic sensory event which is necessary to detect the stimulus omission.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results suggesting functional roles.

claim: Most (88%) caudate neurons with periodic activity exhibited a strong burst of activity around the time of saccades.
source: Most (88%) caudate neurons with periodic activity exhibited a strong burst of activity around the time of saccades, suggesting that they could somehow play a role in eye movement generation.
evidence: Quantitative observation with functional interpretation.

claim: An increase of neuronal firing in the caudate nucleus results in a reduction of activity in the substantia nigra, leading to disinhibition of neurons in the superior colliculus which facilitates saccade generation.
source: It has been widely accepted that an increase of neuronal firing in the caudate nucleus results in a reduction of activity in the substantia nigra, leading to disinhibition of neurons in the superior colliculus which facilitates saccade generation (Hikosaka et al., 2000; Shires et al., 2010).
evidence: Reference to established understanding of basal ganglia circuitry.

claim: Electrical stimulation delivered to the caudate nucleus has been shown to evoke contraversive saccades with short latency (typically < 150 ms).
source: In fact, electrical stimulation delivered to the caudate nucleus has been shown to evoke contraversive saccades with short latency (typically < 150 ms) (Kitama et al., 1991; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: Reference to previously published stimulation studies.

claim: Electrical microstimulation applied to the recording sites failed to elicit immediate saccades but instead reduced the latency of targeting saccades in both directions.
source: In this study, however, electrical microstimulation applied to the recording sites failed to elicit immediate saccades but instead reduced the latency of targeting saccades in both directions.
evidence: Direct report of experimental observation.

claim: The differential stimulation effects might be due to the difference in stimulation sites within the caudate nucleus (i.e. more anterior sites in this study) or the difference in behavioral context.
source: Given that the stimulation parameters in our study was comparable or even stronger than those in the previous studies, the differential stimulation effects might be due to the difference in stimulation sites within the caudate nucleus (i.e. more anterior sites in this study) or the difference in behavioral context (Watanabe and Munoz, 2013).
evidence: Interpretation of differences between current and previous studies.

claim: The effects of electrical stimulation in many sites were evident only when the animals prepared for saccades in response to the stimulus omission.
source: Furthermore, the effects of electrical stimulation in many sites were evident only when the animals prepared for saccades in response to the stimulus omission (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Summary of condition-specific stimulation effects.

claim: Neurons with periodic activity may not directly participate in the triggering of saccades, although they could be related to saccade preparation.
source: These results suggest that neurons with periodic activity may not directly participate in the triggering of saccades, although they could be related to saccade preparation.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Neuronal firing in the primary motor cortex exhibited periodic modulation in anticipation of the trigger signal for reaching movements.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that neuronal firing in the primary motor cortex (Renoult et al., 2006) as well as the power of gamma-band oscillation in the supplementary motor area (Cadena-Valencia et al., 2018) exhibited periodic modulation in anticipation of the trigger signal for reaching movements.
evidence: Reference to previously published findings on motor preparation.

claim: The temporal prediction of repetitive events might be represented by periodic motor preparation in the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry.
source: Considering these results together, the temporal prediction of repetitive events might be represented by periodic motor preparation in the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry.
evidence: Synthesis of current and previous findings into a hypothesis.

claim: The periodic activity was much less when monkeys prepared for saccades in response to the changes in stimulus color.
source: We also found that the periodic activity was much less when monkeys prepared for saccades in response to the changes in stimulus color.
evidence: Direct report of experimental observation.

claim: The different firing modulation was likely attributed to the need for temporal prediction in the missing but not in the deviant conditions.
source: Because the repetitive visual stimuli and required movements were identical between the oddball conditions, the different firing modulation was likely attributed to the need for temporal prediction in the missing but not in the deviant conditions.
evidence: Interpretation of condition-dependent differences in neuronal activity.

claim: The difference in neuronal activity might come from the fact that there was an explicit cue for the timing of the targeting saccade in the deviant condition, while the animals needed to internally determine movement timing for stimulus absence in the missing condition.
source: Alternatively, the difference in neuronal activity might come from the fact that there was an explicit cue for the timing of the targeting saccade in the deviant condition, while the animals needed to internally determine movement timing for stimulus absence in the missing condition.
evidence: Alternative interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Neuronal firing and stimulation effects in several brain areas are different between self-initiated and triggered movements.
source: In relation to this, previous studies have shown that neuronal firing and stimulation effects in several brain areas are different between self-initiated and triggered movements (Kunimatsu et al., 2018; Kunimatsu and Tanaka, 2012; Maimon and Assad, 2006; Ohmae et al., 2017; Turner and Anderson, 2005; van Donkelaar et al., 1999; Zimnik et al., 2019), while significant preparatory activity can be observed when the timing of the trigger signal is certainly predictable (Romo and Schultz, 1992; Tanaka, 2007).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies on movement types.

claim: Neurons in the caudate nucleus modulate firing in association with reward.
source: It is also well documented that neurons in the caudate nucleus modulate firing in association with reward (Kawagoe et al., 1998; Lau and Glimcher, 2007; Lauwereyns et al., 2002; Schultz, 2016).
evidence: Reference to established findings on reward-related activity.

claim: In this study, monkeys obtained an equal amount of reward for every successful trial.
source: However, in this study, monkeys obtained an equal amount of reward for every successful trial.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: The differential modulation of periodic activity between the conditions unlikely reflected reward information.
source: These results indicate that the differential modulation of periodic activity between the conditions unlikely reflected reward information.
evidence: Interpretation based on experimental design.

claim: Different time intervals might be processed by different groups of neurons.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that different time intervals might be processed by different groups of neurons (Hayashi et al., 2015; Heron et al., 2012).
evidence: Reference to previous studies suggesting interval-specific processing.

claim: Neurons in several areas in the cerebral cortex have been shown to exhibit tuned representation of specific intervals during rhythmic movements.
source: In support of this hypothesis, neurons in several areas in the cerebral cortex have been shown to exhibit tuned representation of specific intervals during rhythmic movements (Bartolo et al., 2014; Hayashi et al., 2015; Heron et al., 2012; Merchant et al., 2011).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies showing interval tuning in cortex.

claim: A minority of neurons in the caudate nucleus showed a tuned representation for specific time intervals (200–400 ms), while the majority of neurons exhibited monotonical increase of firing modulation as a function of ISI.
source: We also found in this study that a minority of neurons in the caudate nucleus showed a tuned representation for specific time intervals (200–400 ms, Figure 4B,D), while the majority of neurons exhibited monotonical increase of firing modulation as a function of ISI.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on duration tuning.

claim: Tuned representation for short ISIs was not found in the cerebellar dentate nucleus in the previous study.
source: In contrast, tuned representation for short ISIs was not found in the cerebellar dentate nucleus in the previous study (Ohmae et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to previously published finding.

claim: The duration tuning might only be common in the cortico-basal ganglia pathways but not in the cortico-cerebellar pathways.
source: These results suggest that the duration tuning might only be common in the cortico-basal ganglia pathways but not in the cortico-cerebellar pathways, although alternative possibilities still remain.
evidence: Interpretation of comparative findings with acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: When monitoring a single interval, the time courses of neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex and the striatum are temporally scaled according to the duration of the measured interval.
source: When monitoring a single interval, the time courses of neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex and the striatum are temporally scaled according to the duration of the measured interval (Kunimatsu et al., 2018; Mello et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: Reference to multiple studies showing temporal scaling.

claim: Alteration in the speed of neuronal processing in the population of neurons could be achieved by changing the initial state or the overall level of excitatory input to the recurrent network.
source: Alteration in the speed of neuronal processing in the population of neurons could be achieved by changing the initial state or the overall level of excitatory input to the recurrent network (Murray and Escola, 2017; Suzuki and Tanaka, 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Reference to theoretical and experimental studies on neural mechanisms.

claim: The caudate neurons significantly altered the magnitude of firing modulation for different ISIs.
source: However, the caudate neurons found in the present study significantly altered the magnitude of firing modulation for different ISIs (Figure 4), suggesting that the temporal information processing for periodic events might differ from the scaling representation for single-event timing.
evidence: Experimental observation with interpretation.

claim: Temporally specific gain modulation has been reported in the beta power in the sensorimotor cortices and the neural coherence through the cerebello-cortical pathways during passive listening to isochronous auditory rhythms.
source: Similar to neuronal firing in the caudate and the cerebellar nucleus, temporally specific gain modulation has also been reported in the beta power in the sensorimotor cortices and the neural coherence through the cerebello-cortical pathways during passive listening to isochronous auditory rhythms (Fujioka et al., 2012).
evidence: Reference to previous study showing similar phenomenon in different modality.

claim: The temporally specific gain modulation for periodic timing may be an essential framework to understand neural mechanisms of rhythm perception.
source: The temporally specific gain modulation for periodic timing may be an essential framework to understand neural mechanisms of rhythm perception.
evidence: Interpretive statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: The duration of transient decrements of activity in the cerebellar nucleus was highly dependent on the ISI, while that of transient increases of activity in the caudate nucleus was not.
source: This was because the duration of transient decrements of activity in the cerebellar nucleus was highly dependent on the ISI, while that of transient increases of activity in the caudate nucleus was not (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Explanation of the basis for differential temporal prediction accuracy.

claim: The reaction time in the behavioral paradigm depends both on the latencies of omission detection and saccade generation.
source: Given that the reaction time in our behavioral paradigm depends both on the latencies of omission detection and saccade generation, the different timing of stochastic variation may indicate distinct roles of these subcortical structures; the cerebellum might be responsible for the detection of stimulus omission, while the caudate nucleus might contribute to periodic saccade preparation.
evidence: Logical inference about behavioral components.

claim: Temporal prediction in the caudate nucleus might be represented in motor rather than sensory domain.
source: However, close comparisons of directionality and time course of neuronal activity suggest that temporal prediction in the caudate nucleus might be represented in motor rather than sensory domain.
evidence: Interpretation based on comparative analysis of neuronal properties.

claim: Temporal prediction of alternating imaginary targets recruits gamma-bursts in the supplementary motor area, which appears to reflect periodic motor preparation for reaching.
